Operational notes

Busy-state policy

One flag, src.flask_app.PullState.busy, gates both POST endpoints:

Request

Busy?

Response

POST /pull-data

no

200 {"ok": true, "rows_loaded": n}, or 202 with a background runner

POST /pull-data

yes

409 {"ok": false, "busy": true}; nothing is scraped or written

POST /update-analysis

no

200 {"ok": true, "updated_at": ...}

POST /update-analysis

yes

409 {"ok": false, "busy": true}; the snapshot is left alone

POST /pull-data (loader raised)

–

500 {"ok": false, "error": ...}; the batch was rolled back

POST /update-analysis (database down)

no

503 {"ok": false, "error": ...}; the snapshot is left alone

The flag is set before the job starts and cleared in both the success and the failure path, so a failed pull cannot wedge the pipeline. GET /status exposes the same state as JSON, which is how the page and the tests observe it without polling the database.

Analysis caching

GET /analysis renders the cached snapshot on src.flask_app.PullState, computing one on first visit. A pull does not refresh it – that is what the Update Analysis button is for. The page shows the timestamp of the last update so a stale snapshot is visible rather than silent.

Idempotency and uniqueness

p_id is the primary key and is derived from the record rather than generated by the database (src.load_data.derive_p_id()):

  1. an explicit p_id or id on the record, if it is an integer;

  2. otherwise the numeric id in the Grad Café result URL (.../result/1020482 → 1020482);

  3. otherwise a SHA-256 fingerprint of program, comments, date_added and status, reduced to a 31-bit integer.

Inserts use ON CONFLICT (p_id) DO NOTHING, so:

  • pulling the same page twice inserts nothing the second time;

  • overlapping pulls insert only the records the database has not seen;

  • src.load_data.insert_rows() returns the number of genuinely new rows, which is what the endpoint reports as rows_loaded.

Failure handling

The whole batch is one transaction. Any psycopg.Error rolls it back and re-raises, so a bad row in the middle of a pull cannot leave a partial write behind. The endpoint turns that into a 500 and records the message on the state, where the page renders it as an error banner.

Required fields

src.load_data.REQUIRED_FIELDS lists the columns that may never be NULL. src.load_data.normalize_record() fills each of them with a documented fallback ("Unknown", "Applied", "Other", ""), and the table declares them NOT NULL so the guarantee is enforced where it matters.

Background pulls

The default runner is synchronous: the response arrives after the load finishes. Passing runner=run_in_thread to src.flask_app.create_app() moves the job to a daemon thread; the endpoint then answers 202 and the caller watches GET /status for completion.

Degraded mode

GET /analysis never fails with a 500 because the database is down. If psycopg.OperationalError is raised while computing the analysis or reading rows, the page still renders: both buttons work, every question is listed, the answers read N/A or 0, and a banner (data-testid="db-error") explains that PostgreSQL is unreachable and how to check it. POST /update-analysis answers 503 in the same situation, and POST /pull-data answers 500, because those are real failed actions rather than a page that can degrade.

The loader behaves the same way at the command line: src.load_data.main() catches the connection failure, prints src.load_data.CONNECTION_HELP to stderr with the three things to check, loads nothing, and returns 1 so the process exits non-zero.
